newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Albright links Bosnia aid to cooperation by parties.
newsitem.headline: Albright links Bosnia aid to cooperation by parties.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Sunday her government remained committed to building a lasting peace in Bosnia as long as the former war factions showed a willingness to cooperate.
During a visit to the Bosnian capital Sarajevo, Albright invoked the memory of America's Marshall Plan after World War Two as she pledged U.S. support for reconstruction efforts.
"What is happening here in Sarajevo is the modern day version of a Marshall Plan where America provides assistance, but it provides assistance to those who help themselves," she told reporters.
She said U.S. aid could dry up if Bosnia's political leaders did not uphold their obligations under the Dayton peace accords.
Albright earlier took a stroll down the notorious former "Sniper's Alley" where Sarajevans once dodged bullets during the nationalist Serb siege of the city.
"There is a great deal to be done but let us never forget that three years ago people were still dying on these streets and we would not be able to be taking these kind of walks," she said.
Albright's visit coincided with growing international concern that the fragile peace is unravelling, only a year before the NATO-led peace force is due to withdraw.

She met Bosnian Moslem, Croat and Serb members of the collective presidency as part of a U.S. effort to bolster the 1995 peace agreement, which ended four years of war in former Yugoslavia but has not created a vital spirit of co-existence and reconciliation.

Nationalist authorities in Bosnia, trying to seal the results of wartime "ethnic cleansing", have prevented refugees from returning to their homes and flouted other key provisions of the treaty, notably the extradition of indicted war criminals.

Albright flew to Sarajevo a day after delivering stern warnings to leaders of Bosnia's powerful neighbours, Croatia and Serbia, which armed and steered the war efforts of the Bosnian Croats and Serbs respectively.

In blunt language, Albright reprimanded presidents Franjo Tudjman of Croatia and Slobodan Milosevic of Serbia for failing to hand over war-crimes indictees and dragging their feet on other key aspects of the U.S.-brokered peace agreement.
She called for Milosevic, a key signatory of the U.S.- brokered Dayton accords, to stop "stonewalling" and cooperate with the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague.

She said Milosevic needed to secure the extradition of former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic, who still wields power in Serb-controlled territory from his offices in Pale, 16 km (10 miles) outside Sarajevo.
In Zagreb, Albright said she told Tudjman that he must prevent violence against minority Serb war refugees trying to return to Croatia and to cooperate with the U.N. tribunal.

Albright said on Sunday that the continued presence of war crimes suspects in Bosnia represented a "major roadblock to progress" but offered no details about how Washington intended to resolve the problem.
"The United States is looking into options to strengthen the work of the war crimes tribunal," she said, without elaborating.
Albright joined Sarajevo police officers as they walked their "beat" to show her support for canton authorities who have restructured the police force based on United Nations guidelines.
Although city authorities have integrated non-Moslems into their police force, U.N. monitors have expressed concern over a spate of beatings by Sarajevo police over the past few months.
Albright was scheduled to fly by helicopter later on Sunday to the disputed northern town of Brcko, considered one of the country's most volatile flashpoints.
She planned to meet U.S. soldiers stationed in Brcko before heading to the northwestern town of Banja Luka, where she was due to hold talks with Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic.
